text:
Trump EPA Celebrates Children’s Health Month with 100 Actions to Protect the Nation’s Most Precious Resource
WASHINGTON — The Trump Administration has been racking up huge wins when it comes to protecting children’s health. In honor of Children's Health Month, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released a list of 100 actions taken to protect children’s health and secure America’s future.
Since January 2025, the Trump EPA has taken actions that protect children’s health by reducing lead and PFAS exposure, enhancing chemical and pesticide safety, improving air quality, and growing state and local partnerships to Make America Healthy Again. The list of 100 actions to help safeguard American children illustrates this EPA’s unwavering commitment to the health and wellbeing of American families.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, EPA is focused on delivering clean air, land, and water for every American child,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, “This doesn’t just mean reducing lead exposure or more quickly cleaning up toxic sites, it also involves giving families peace of mind by equipping them with the knowledge and tools they need to keep their kids safe.”
For Children’s Health Month 2026, EPA’s educational efforts revolve around three main priorities:
- Raise Awareness: Know the environmental risks that can affect children’s health.
- Act Early: Reduce hazards in the places children live, learn, and play.
- Protect and Prevent: Support healthy environments for every child, every day.
EPA urges families, schools, and communities to learn more about children’s environmental health and use available resources to reduce exposures, support prevention, and promote healthier communities for children across the country. Children’s Health Month also includes National Lead Poisoning Prevention Week, an important opportunity to raise awareness and take action to prevent lead exposures, especially in children.
Here are 100 actions EPA has taken since January 20, 2025, to protect children’s health:
- Provided $2.9 billion in funding for states to reduce lead in drinking water through the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF).
- Worked with more than 100 drinking water systems to guide them through the process of lead service line removal through the Get the Lead Out technical assistance initiative.
- Released several tools to help states and water systems prepare for new requirements in the Lead and Copper Rule related to lead sampling in schools and childcare facilities. These tools include a resource guide, sampling waiver checklists, and frequently asked questions.
- Released a Lead and Children’s Health StoryMap to highlight information on national trends on lead and help ensure families stay healthy and safe.
- Released an Asthma & Children’s Health StoryMap to provide information on how environmental factors, such as air quality, affect health outcomes like asthma rates and other conditions.
- Updated the America’s Children and the Environment (ACE) data and trends tool to better present children’s environmental health data to non-technical audiences
- Updated the Children’s Unique Vulnerabilities to Environmental Hazards resource to include exposure examples across life stages and provides a more comprehensive picture of children’s health issues through life stages and windows of susceptibility.
- Updated the Children’s Environmental Health Facts resource to provide key facts and statistics and highlight trends and economic impacts of childhood health concerns.
- Released a resource for parents about how to protect children from elemental mercury, What to Do If You Find or Spill Mercury.
- Updated Sensible Steps to Healthier School Environments to address common areas of environmental health concerns in schools and provide information about existing low-cost or no-cost measures, programs, and resources that are available to help prevent, reduce, and resolve hazards.
- Highlighted children’s health on EPA’s Research Partner Support Stories, including science-based information to communities, families, caretakers, and school decision makers to protect children’s health and reduce environmental exposures to harmful contaminants.
- Presented information to the Colorado Association of Libraries about EPA Region 8’s Community Libraries Program, which offers an extensive inventory of information and resources related to protecting the health of children and indoor air, childhood lead poisoning prevention, and other environmental education assistance.
- Published four quarterly EPA Mountains & Plains Regional Healthy Schools Newsletter editions shared with EPA Region 8’s network of healthy schools contacts.
- Formed a Senior Lead Leadership Coordinating Committee to strengthen cross-agency efforts to reduce lead exposure and protect children from lead-related health risks, meeting EPA’s commitments under the Federal Lead Action Plan.
- Completed a Federal Lead Resources Guide for use by partners and the public, in particular with other federal departments and agencies.
- Published the updated Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home pamphlet in multiple languages in collaboration with federal and state partners.
- Launched revamped lead website (epa.gov/lead) to streamline navigation and serve as a one-stop shop for EPA information on lead and quickly connect users to resources, tools and guidance.
- Hosted in-person and virtual educational sessions on the Lead Awareness Curriculum about the dangers of lead, and ways to reduce and prevent lead exposure and equip community leaders to educate their communities about lead.
- Hosted virtual National Meeting on EPA’s Lead-Based Paint Program for authorized Tribal and state programs and non-authorized state programs.
- Facilitated a webinar, Lead-Based Paint Awareness for Building Code Officials, on lead-based paint regulations.
- Published materials in collaboration with federal partners for individuals, communities and Tribal, state and local governments and organizations ("partners") to use to raise awareness during National Lead Poisoning Prevention Week.
- Published updated materials for the EPA/HUD Lead Dust Sampling Technician and Certified Renovator model courses as part of EPA’s implementation of the Reconsideration of the Dust-Lead Hazard Standards and Dust-Lead Post-Abatement Clearance Levels Rule.
- Released new guidance to reduce lead exposure in drinking water and help drinking water systems protect American children.
- Worked with states and federal partners to implement the Lead-Free Rule and reduce lead in pipes, plumbing fittings, and fixtures used for drinking water.
- Increased awareness among property management companies with lead safety requirements under the Lead Renovation Repair and Painting (RRP) Rule and the Real Estate Notification and Lead Disclosure Rule to protect military families living in privatized military housing.
- Issued the Residential Lead Directive for CERCLA Sites and RCRA Hazardous Waste Cleanup Program Facilities to accelerate lead cleanup at contaminated sites.
- Published a new webpage that provides healthy gardening practices for residents living in areas where soil may be contaminated with lead.
- Hosted public meetings in Colorado for community members to discuss lead and arsenic contamination in soils from historic smelters, including educational materials on lead exposure reduction.
- Advanced lead testing and remediation in schools and childcare settings across states and Tribal communities through Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation (WIIN) grant funding.
- Published a mapping blueprint for identifying locations in the United States for focusing high-impact interventions to reduce childhood lead exposure.
- Developed a resource list on lead risks in ammunition and fishing tackle to increase awareness about this exposure route and its impact on children’s health.
- Presented information about how to organize a soilSHOP health education community event that offers free soil lead screenings and education about how to reduce lead exposures to children and families at the EPA Tools & Resources August national webinar.
- Convened lead listening sessions in EPA Region 1 with state public health and environmental agencies in New England in partnership with the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO).
- Worked with partners in EPA Region 2 – including Families for Lead Freedom Now, the New York State Department of Health (NYSDOH), and the City of Syracuse – to develop stronger community relationships and community engagement materials on the Lead and Copper Rule.
- Held an inaugural lead workshop in San Juan, Puerto Rico – in collaboration with the Puerto Rico Department of Health, Region 2 Pediatric Environmental Health Specialty Unit (PEHSU), Puerto Rico Department of Environmental and Natural Resources, College of Engineers and Surveyors of Puerto Rico (CIAPR), and engineering partners – to teach construction workers how to prevent lead exposure at home.
- Hosted an availability session with local partners in EPA Region 2 – including the Puerto Rico Department of Health, Municipality of Vega Baja, and College of Medical Technologists – to conduct capillary lead tests for residents and children who attended the event.
- Worked with state departments of health in EPA Region 3 to determine needs regarding blood lead level testing and provided education to medical providers.
- Funded Lead Renovation Repair and Painting trainings in Region 6 locations to increase compliance awareness and prevent lead exposure to children.
- Increased compliance among states in EPA Region 9 to complete lead service line inventories.
- Issued the National Perchloroethylene Air Emission Standards for Dry Cleaning Facilities to reduce air pollution that can affect children’s health.
- Updated the Wildfire Smoke: A Guide for Public Health Officials, which included children’s health considerations.
- Hosted webinars for schools on ventilation, improved indoor air quality, and wildfire smoke to support school air quality planning and maintenance.
- Supported the PEHSU Asthma Home Visit Program in EPA Region 8, helping children with persistent asthma reduce triggers in their homes.
- Partnered with libraries and firefighters to provide Do-It-Yourself air cleaner demonstrations and asthma education to communities experiencing wildfire smoke in EPA Region 10.
- Awarded funding to Maine Department of Health and Human Services to support radon testing in Maine Schools.
- Added an additional PFAS to the Toxics Release Inventory reporting list.
- Published draft guidance to help wastewater utilities, landowners, and the public reduce risk from PFOA and PFOS in biosolids.
- EPA laboratory methods to measure microplastics in drinking water, helping decision-makers address microplastic pollution closer to its source.
- Published the final risk evaluation for 1,3-butadiene, which found unreasonable risks for some industrial settings that could lead to health risks for workers, including reduced birthweight pregnancies.
- Proposed a draft risk evaluation on octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane (D4), finding unreasonable risks for some industrial settings and a consumer use that could lead to effects related to reproductive outcomes.
- Published the final risk evaluations for six phthalates – dibutyl phthalate (1,2-benzene- dicarboxylic acid, 1,2- dibutyl ester) (DBP), butyl benzyl phthalate (1,2-benzene- dicarboxylic acid, 1- butyl 2(phenylmethyl) ester) (BBP), diisobutyl phthalate (1,2-benzene- dicarboxylic acid, 1,2- bis-(2methylpropyl) ester) (DIBP), dicyclohexyl phthalate (DCHP), and diethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) – finding unreasonable risks for some industrial settings that could lead to health risks for workers, including hormone deficiencies and endocrine disruption.
- Proposed a draft risk evaluation on p-dichlorobenzene (pDCB), finding unreasonable risks for some workers and consumers, including air care products that could lead to exposures to children and potential health risks of neurotoxicity and developmental toxicity.
- Proposed a draft risk evaluation on 1,3,4,6,7,8-hexahydro-4,6,6,7,8,8-hexamethylcyclopenta [g]-2-benzopyran (HHCB), finding the most sensitive effects are developmental effects on offspring growth.
- Supported the Trump Administration’s continued efforts to crackdown on illegal toxic pesticides and chemical smuggling operations. EPA, joined by the U.S. Customs and Border Protection, inspected five seaports and land ports of entry across the country and identified thousands of violative products that are regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act and EPA’s Lead Free Rule.
- Published a study – Laboratory investigation of inadvertently generated PCBs released from consumer products into lake water – investigating the occurrence and leaching behavior of inadvertently generated polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), prioritizing consumer products used by children, to better understand exposure risks.
- Published a study – Proteome profiling of emamectin-treated primary rat cortical cells following up to twelve days in vitro exposure – identifying altered protein biochemical processes that may inform mechanisms of developmental neurotoxicity related to chemical exposures.
- Published a study – Single-cell RNA sequencing of human embryonic stem cells reveals immediate and deferred transcriptomic responses to retinoic acid-mediated effects across cell subpopulations – used single-cell sequencing techniques to assess the utility of the method for understanding developmental changes related to chemical exposures for potential use in screening paradigms.
- Issued Current Progress and Research Needs to Protect Children’s Environmental Health to summarize research and policy opportunities advancing children’s environmental health.
- Led work with the President’s Task Force on Environmental Health Risks and Safety Risks to Children to improve communications and coordinate federal children’s health efforts.
- Contributed to annual reports from the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics.
- Created a Children’s Environmental Health Workgroup through the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) to share information and best practices.
- Supported state lead program prevention programs through sharing resources and identifying areas for collaboration.
- Provided information to state officials about the Pediatric Environmental Health Specialty Units (PEHSUs) across the country.
- Supported a removal action in Massachusetts in EPA Region 1 to address lead and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) contamination in soil where families and children live.
- Worked with partners in EPA Region 5 in state and local governments and organizations to create a network of neighborhood-level air quality monitoring stations in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, focusing on neighborhoods with high asthma burdens for children and adults to improve asthma awareness.
- Held two mercury trainings in EPA Region 5 in Marion County, Ohio, focused on children’s safety, proper response procedure and tactics for local responders, and mercury health risks.
- Hosted a Children’s Health Seminar with the Arkansas Department of Health and Region 6 PEHSU to strengthen the state’s ability to identify and address environmental health risks affecting children.
- Hosted a Children’s Environmental Health Symposium in Region 6 in partnership with Children’s Health Hospital of Dallas educating pediatric providers and nurses on environmental risks that can affect children’s health.
- Worked in partnership with the Region 6 Border Program and PEHSU to train pediatric health care providers and community health workers along the U.S.-Mexico Border on children’s health topics such as Community Emergency Preparedness and Household Hazardous Chemicals.
- Trained Head Start Family Resource Specialists in Region 6 on environmental risks to children, particularly the importance of both preventing lead exposure and childhood blood lead level testing.
- Coordinated with the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services in EPA Region 8 to provide EPA resources in a four-part webinar series on reducing environmental exposures for early childcare providers.
- Provided children’s environmental health and disaster preparedness education by helping children pack “Grab and Go” bags at a Tribal event for National Emergency Preparedness Month across EPA Region 10.
- Completed the Schools Adapting to Natural Disasters project, including an assessment for Gary Community School Corporation and a technical guidance playbook for Broward County Public Schools.
- Coordinated the internal Children’s Health Activities and Research Group at EPA (CHARGE) to improve implementation, communication, and collaboration across EPA.
- Presented EPA's Air Quality Flag Program to tribes raising awareness about air quality and its related children impacts to children's health and recruited new partners across the country.
- Worked with Tribal, federal, and state partners to characterize uranium mine sites, communicate risks, develop response plans, and address contaminated homes on Tribal lands.
- Provided technical expertise on air pollutants associated with chronic respiratory health impacts, including PM2.5, ozone, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and wood-stove emissions, and led learning activities for the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe’s “Preserving Our Homeland” summer camp.
- Partnered with the Shinnecock Nation of Indian's Environmental Department to develop an air quality education program with the Shinnecock Boys and Girls Club and local elementary schools and libraries to review the Air Quality Index, showcase PM 2.5 purple air sensors, and lead an Air Quality Index activity with air quality flags.
- Hosted a Children’s Environmental Health educational session at a Choctaw Nation Summit, highlighting lead-based paint, household hazardous chemicals, and air quality.
- Hosted a Healthy Homes practical training on assessing and addressing health and safety risks in homes, including risks specific to children of tribal members, in partnership with the Meskwaki Nation.
- Promoted the Air Quality Flag Program to recruit new Tribal partners in Region 6 and Region 8.
- Assisted Tribal Drinking Water Systems throughout Region 9 to complete lead service line inventories.
- Funded the replacement of water storage tanks containing lead paint in the Tohono O'odham Nation.
- Provided technical assistance to drinking water systems on Tohono O’odham and Navajo lands with lead exceedances to provide public notification and comply with Lead and Copper Rule requirements.
- Took action to address uranium contamination in the Southwest and its intergenerational neurodevelopmental health effects on the Navajo Nation and surrounding Tribal communities.
- Educated Tribal leaders on actions they could take to help protect children from environmental health risks at the Region 9 Tribal Operations Committee meeting.
- Launched the Feed It Onward initiative to combat food waste, helping to ensure food is being used in productive ways, like feeding children and families, instead of ending up in landfills.
- Advanced a comprehensive PFAS strategy by highlighting innovative PFAS treatment and destruction technologies, announcing nearly $1 billion in new funding to states to address PFAS in drinking water, and issuing two proposed rules for public comment that uphold the National Primary Drinking Water Standards (NPDWS) for PFOA and PFOS.
- Launched the PFAS OUTreach—or PFAS OUT—initiative to proactively work with communities and water systems to reduce exposure to PFOA and PFOS in drinking water, years ahead of compliance with federal regulatory requirements.
- Announced a joint initiative to mark first-ever inclusion of microplastics on EPA's Contaminant Candidate List, launching the groundbreaking Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) program to detect and remove plastics from the human body.
- Announced a joint plan with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and Department of Agriculture (USDA) to provide over $1 billion in investments on farm modernization and long-term food supply security.
- Sought public input on a national innovation challenge to find safer, science-based alternatives to chemical crop desiccation in a win for American families and farmers.
- Announced the next step in the review of public health risks linked to fluoride in drinking water by releasing the Protocol for Developing the Fluoride Human Health Toxicity Assessment.
- Announced $30 million in grant funding under EPA’s Real Water Technical Assistance Initiative, to provide training and technical assistance that will improve water quality in small and rural communities across America.
- Took key steps to advance Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) implementation by proposing to monitor contaminants that are not currently regulated but may be present in drinking water in the Sixth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 6).
- Developed two drinking water PFAS treatment models and a cost estimating tool for drinking water systems to understand the planning level costs for installing treatment to remove PFAS from drinking water.
- Provided comprehensive training to state agencies and technical assistance providers to support effective implementation of the 2024 PFAS drinking water regulation, which is designed to reduce exposure to contaminants that may increase the risk of developmental effects during childhood.
- Released human health benchmarks for 374 pharmaceuticals including separate benchmarks for infants and the general population. These benchmarks provide states, Tribes, and local water systems with information to identify pharmaceutical levels that may warrant further monitoring or research, helping inform efforts to protect children’s health.
- Awarding the 2026 National Environmental Leaders in Asthma recognition to the City of San Antonio Metropolitan Health Department’s San Antonio Kids BREATHE (SAKB) program.
- Requested $6.8 million to co-lead the President’s Task Force on Environmental Health Risks to Children, support Pediatric Environmental Health Specialty Units, and enhance monitoring of children’s health trends in the Fiscal Year 2027 President’s Budget.

Russian National Arrested and Extradited to New York on Charges of Evading Sanctions on Russia
Alexander Suvorov, 52, a Russian national, has been charged by a criminal complaint with three counts related to the unlawful exporting of micro-electronic components from the United States to Russia via a front company based in Hong Kong.
“Those, like the defendant, as alleged, who seek to enrich themselves by evading economic sanctions on Russia, must understand that their actions carry serious consequences and will not be tolerated,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III for the Northern District of New York. “My office, working together with the FBI and the Department of Commerce, will continue to aggressively prosecute these types of cases and hold offenders accountable to the fullest extent of the law. This historic extradition shows that we will fly over 3,800 miles to locate and bring to justice those who threaten national security.”
“Alexander Suvorov was the alleged mastermind behind an international procurement network that illegally supplied buyers in Russia with American-made electronic components that have military applications,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “His extradition to face charges here in the U.S. demonstrates the FBI's commitment to keeping sensitive, export-controlled technology out of the hands of the Russian military. We will continue working with our law enforcement, intelligence, private sector, and international partners to bring to justice all who attempt to arm our adversaries at the expense of our citizens and our national security.”
“The Bureau of Industry and Security is committed to strong enforcement,” said Special Agent in Charge Jonathan Carson of the U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security New York Field Office. “Working closely with out law enforcement partners, we will continue to uncover and disrupt illicit procurement and diversion networks wherever they operate.”
Suvorov was extradited from Sweden to the Northern District of New York on Oct. 15 and is expected to have his initial appearance on Oct. 16 in Albany, New York.
The complaint filed against Suvorov alleges that between about March 2022 and April 2023, Suvorov led an illicit procurement network responsible for unlawfully exporting U.S. electronic components out of the United States to Russia. One of the procurement network’s main goals was to fraudulently obtain dual-use electronic components — that is, electronic components with both civilian and military applications — from U.S. companies for shipment to Russia. As alleged in the complaint, Suvorov’s primary role in the procurement network was to maintain front companies based in Hong Kong, including GS Group Limited, which the procurement network used to order electronic components from U.S. companies in an effort to conceal that the end users of the components were in Russia, and to then transship, via Hong Kong, the components from the U.S. companies to the end users in Russia. Suvorov and his companies are also alleged to have sent multiple wires to various U.S. companies to pay for the electronic components. Some of the components unlawfully purchased and exported to Russia by Suvorov and his procurement network can be used in military communication and radar systems, as well as precision location systems.
Count 1 of the complaint alleges conspiracy to commit international promotional money laundering and carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $500,000. Count 2 alleges conspiracy to commit outbound smuggling and carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $250,000. Count 3 alleges conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act (ECRA) and carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $1,000,000. A federal district judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
The FBI and Department of Commerce are investigating the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs secured the extradition of Suvorov with the assistance of the Swedish Authorities.
Trial Attorney Garrett Coyle of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Rick Belliss for the Northern District of New York are prosecuting the case.

Sánchez, Sewell lead 55 Democrats in opposing U.S. Withdrawal from International Labor Organization
ILO withdrawal would weaken international labor standards, undercut American workers
WASHINGTON – Ways and Means Trade Subcommittee Ranking Member Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.) and Oversight Subcommittee Ranking Member Terri Sewell (D-Ala.) today led 55 of their House Democratic colleagues in calling on the Trump administration to maintain United States participation in the International Labor Organization (ILO), which brings together governments, workers and employers to establish international labor standards. Those standards help protect American workers from being undercut by other countries with weaker labor standards.
Reports that the administration is considering withdrawal come amid a severe budget crisis at the ILO, driven largely by the Trump administration’s failure to pay approximately $300 million in outstanding U.S. membership dues.
“At the same time that the Administration has called on countries to improve labor standards, it is reportedly considering a withdrawal from the very institution that develops those standards and helps governments implement them,” the members wrote. “Notably, USTR relied on ILO data in conducting [its Section 301] investigations, underscoring the organization’s value to U.S. efforts to identify and combat forced labor.
“If the Administration believes that weak labor standards distort trade and disadvantage American workers and firms, withdrawing from an institution whose standards, research, and expertise it relies upon to address those concerns runs counter to American interests.”
In addition to Sánchez and Sewell, the letter was signed by Representatives Gabe Amo (D-R.I.), Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.), Donald Beyer (D-Va.), Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), Judy Chu (D-Calif.), Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), Danny Davis (D-Ill.), Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.), Christopher Deluzio (D-Pa.), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.), Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), Dwight Evans (D-Pa.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.), Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Val Hoyle (D-Ore.), Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.), William Keating (D-Mass.), Robin Kelly (D-Ill.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), Greg Landsman (D-Ohio), John Larson (D-Conn.), Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), John Mannion (D-N.Y.), Morgan McGarvey (D-Ky.), James McGovern (D-Mass.), Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), Gwen Moore (D-Wis.), Richard Neal (D-Mass.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), Stacey Plaskett (D-V.I.), Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), Nellie Pou (D-N.J.), Emily Randall (D-Wash.), Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.), Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.), Robert Scott (D-Va.), Terri Sewell (D-Ala.), Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.), Thomas Suozzi (D-N.Y.), Mike Thompson (D-Calif.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.), Norma Torres (D-Calif.), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) and Frederica Wilson (D-Fla.).
The full text of the letter is available HERE and follows:
October 15, 2026
Secretary Rubio
U.S. Department of State
2201 C Street NW
Washington, D.C. 20520
Dear Secretary Rubio:
We write to express our deep concern regarding reports that the Administration is preparing to withdraw the United States from the International Labor Organization (ILO). Such a decision would undermine the organization’s core mission of establishing and promoting international labor standards in the global economy and would be difficult to reconcile with the Administration’s stated pro-worker trade agenda. These reports come amid a severe budget crisis at the ILO, which is largely due to the Administration’s failure to pay approximately $300 million in outstanding U.S. membership dues. Unlike most international organizations, the ILO’s unique tripartite structure gives governments, workers, and employers the central role of developing international labor standards to combat the global “race to the bottom” that has undermined wages and working conditions here in the United States and around the globe.
The labor standards developed and articulated by the constituents of the ILO underpin the labor provisions in U.S. trade agreements, which require trading partners to adopt, maintain, and effectively enforce labor laws related to eliminating forced labor, child labor, and employment discrimination, while also protecting workers’ fundamental right to organize unions and bargain collectively. Such obligations are vital to levelling the playing field by preventing other countries from gaining an unfair advantage through common forms of labor exploitation. But negotiated commitments are only as effective as the institutions that implement them. For decades, the ILO has helped governments put these commitments into practice through technical assistance, training, advisory services, reporting, investigations, and capacity-building support to labor inspectorates.
Several U.S. trading partners have reportedly sought ILO assistance in response to the Administration’s recent imposition of Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies for failing to impose or effectively enforce prohibitions on imports produced with forced labor. Other partners have sought to extend ILO programming that is a key U.S. trade condition for access to the U.S. market. Yet, at the same time that the Administration has called on countries to improve labor standards, it is reportedly considering a withdrawal from the very institution that develops those standards and helps governments implement them. Notably, USTR relied on ILO data in conducting these investigations, underscoring the organization’s value to U.S. efforts to identify and combat forced labor. If the Administration believes that weak labor standards distort trade and disadvantage American workers and firms, withdrawing from an institution whose standards, research, and expertise it relies upon to address those concerns runs counter to American interests.
The ILO’s value extends beyond government enforcement and directly benefits American companies operating in global supply chains. Through programs such as Better Work, a joint initiative of the ILO and the International Finance Corporation, factories receive auditing, training, and support to improve compliance with national laws and international labor standards. Improved transparency at the factory level enables companies to identify risks in their supply chains, address problems before they become more serious, and avoid reputational damage through responsible sourcing practices. The American Apparel & Footwear Association and other U.S. business organizations recently highlighted the important role of the ILO in strengthening labor enforcement in sourcing countries, addressing forced labor, and maintaining a competitive environment for American companies and workers.
The ILO’s role in advancing U.S. trade policy is well illustrated in Haiti, where U.S. law ties preferential market access to labor law compliance and integrates the ILO into that statutory framework. In September, Congress reauthorized the Haitian Hemispheric Opportunity through Partnership Encouragement Act (HOPE) and the Haiti Economic Lift Program Act (HELP). Under these programs, Haiti is mandated to work with the ILO to implement the Technical Assistance Improvement and Compliance Needs Assessment and Remediation (TAICNAR) program. The ILO’s Better Work program in Haiti operates the core compliance component of TAICNAR, conducting factory assessments, supporting remediation, and providing technical assistance to strengthen industrial relations and labor law enforcement. If the ILO is unable to continue performing these functions, Haiti will be unable to meet the labor compliance requirements Congress established as a condition of these trade preferences—programs that continue to enjoy strong bipartisan support.
Finally, the United States withdrawal from the ILO will only serve to expand China’s influence at the organization and deprive us of a key forum for holding them accountable for systemic labor rights violations. For example, in 2022 the United States delegation to the ILO’s annual conference played a decisive role in rallying support from governments, workers, and employers to condemn China’s use of forced labor camps to “re-educate” Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in China's Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR). A U.S. withdrawal will not halt the development of international labor standards; rather, it will strip American policymakers, workers, and employers of their ability to shape their creation and implementation in a manner that reflects our values. Walking away cedes strategic leverage to a major economic competitor over the very rules that govern fair competition in the global marketplace. This exposure is particularly critical as the ILO facilitates the development of standards for emerging issues, including the platform economy, artificial intelligence, and workplace health and safety. American workers and companies will ultimately be impacted by these international standards, regardless of whether the United States chooses to participate in their creation.
Accordingly, we urge the Administration to maintain full United States membership in the ILO and utilize appropriated Contributions to International Organizations (CIO) funds to expeditiously pay the approximately $300 million in arrears. Abandoning the ILO does not protect American interests. Instead, it diminishes our ability to enforce trade agreements, taints our supply chains, and hands a strategic victory to our economic competitors. The United States must maintain its seat at the table to ensure that global labor standards are driven by American values, interests, and priorities.
To assist Congress in monitoring the implementation of U.S. trade policy and funding mandates, please provide comprehensive responses to the following questions by October 30, 2026:
- Given the Administration’s extensive reliance on ILO data to execute recent Section 301 tariff enforcement actions, what concrete steps is the Department of State taking to ensure the ILO remains fully funded and operationally viable so that U.S. trade enforcement mechanisms are not compromised?
- Because Congress has explicitly tied preferential market access for Haiti to the execution of the TAICNAR program, what immediate actions is the Department taking to ensure that the U.S. remains fully engaged in the ILO framework so as not to jeopardize the legal compliance of these congressional trade preferences?
- In alignment with the 2025 National Security Strategy’s mandate to protect American workers from foreign economic distortion, what is the Department’s explicit plan to utilize the United States' permanent seat on the ILO Governing Body to actively counter China's expanding influence over global standard-setting?
- Out of funds appropriated by Congress under the CIO account for Fiscal Years 2024, 2025, and 2026, what is the exact timeline for the Department to release the necessary funds to clear the outstanding $300 million in arrears and stabilize U.S. standing and voting rights within the organization?

EPA to Provide Update on Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, Including, a Planned Wall to Contain Contaminated Groundwater
EPA to Provide Update on Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, Including, a Planned Wall to Contain Contaminated Groundwater
GAINESVILLE, Florida (Oct. 15, 2026) – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will hold an open house on Wednesday, Oct. 21 from 5 – 7 p.m. at the Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, 200 NW 23rd Avenue in Gainesville, Florida, to share an update on cleanup activities, including installation of a 5,300-foot wall extending 65 feet below ground to help prevent contaminated groundwater and soil from spreading.
Additional actions, planned in coordination with local, state, and federal partners, include:
- Replacing existing stormwater ditch with a new piping system configured to avoid the groundwater cut-off wall.
- Removing contaminated soil piles, surface soil, and ditch sediments from former Municipal Storage Yard and relocating them inside the cut-off wall.
Background
The Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site encompasses 140 acres in Gainesville, Florida. The Cabot portion of the site operated as a pine-tar products facility from 1910 until 1967 and has been redeveloped into commercial properties. Cleanup on this portion is mostly complete and includes a separate cut-off wall to prevent contaminated water and soil from leaking out. The Koppers site operated as a wood treatment facility from 1916 until 2009. This site is owned by Beazer East, Inc. and is undergoing cleanup. Under a consent decree with EPA, Beazer East has certain cleanup responsibilities for a portion of the site.
###
title: EPA to Provide Update on Cabot/Koppers Superfund Site, Including, a Planned Wall to Contain Contaminated Groundwater

Congresswoman Dina Titus introduced legislation today to require the Department of Transportation to examine whether it can strengthen fuel efficiency requirements to counter high gas prices and reinstate penalties for automakers that fail to produce fuel-efficient vehicles.
“With gas prices skyrocketing because of President Trump’s prolonged and illegal war, we must take immediate steps to give American consumers some relief,” Congresswoman Titus said. “In May 2026, gas prices rose at a rate ten times higher than the rate of inflation. In Nevada, they now average $5.45 per gallon. Coupled with higher prices on groceries and other goods because of the Trump tariffs, families are struggling to make ends meet.”
Congresswoman Titus, a member of the House Transportation Committee. and co-sponsor Doris Matsui, (CA-7), a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, introduced the Gas Money Saved Act to review Corporate Fuel Economy (CAFÉ) standards and reinstate fuel-efficiency requirements that were stripped away by Republicans’ Big Ugly Bill in 2025. Companion legislation has been introduced in the Senate by Senator Ed Markey (D-MA).
“These giveaways to Big Oil and automakers worsened the pain at the pump and should not stand,” Congresswoman Titus said. 
“Fuel economy standards help American drivers get around without breaking the bank while gas prices are high, but Trump and the Republicans gutted these standards as part of their crusade to put Big Oil above American families,” said Senator Markey. “Auto innovation should give consumers better choices, not cut corners at their expense. The Gas Money Saved Act would make sure American drivers have fuel-efficient vehicle options that are cheaper to fill up and hold automakers to account—a cost-saving measure that is especially critical as the Trump Administration would rather spend billions on an illegal war than keep costs low for Americans.”
“Across the country, Americans are being squeezed by high gas prices, rising grocery bills, and everyday costs that keep stretching family budgets thinner,” said Congresswoman Matsui. “The Gas Money Saved Act meets people where they are by strengthening fuel efficiency standards that help drivers spend less on gas for years to come. This is a practical step to lower everyday costs, give families more breathing room, and build a cleaner, more efficient transportation future.”
The Gas Money Saved Act would:
    - Require DOT to reevaluate Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE)standards if gas prices rise at a rate five times faster than inflation over a six-month period, and;
- Restore and increase financial penalties on automakers if their car and truck fleet does not meet fuel efficiency standards.
###
title: Rep. Dina Titus Introduces Legislation to Protect Americans from High Costs at the Pump

Florida Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Opioid Distribution Conspiracy
A Miami, Florida man pleaded guilty yesterday for his role in a conspiracy to distribute over 87,000 oxycodone 30mg pills.
According to court documents and statements made in court, Jose Llerena, 49, of Miami, Florida, conspired with others, including Olushola Yusuf—a pharmacist and pharmacy owner convicted at trial earlier this year for illegally dispensing over 300,000 oxycodone 30mg pills—to illegally distribute oxycodone to individuals who had no medical need for the drug. Llerena was a “patient recruiter” who paid individuals to pose as patients and obtain illegal and unnecessary oxycodone prescriptions from South Florida clinics and doctors. Llerena then took his recruits and their illegal prescriptions to Yusuf’s pharmacies in order to get the pills. Yusuf kept a list of Llerena’s recruits at her pharmacy. Llerena paid Yusuf cash for the drug at above market value.
List Seized by Law Enforcement from Yusuf’s Pharmacy of Purported “Patients” Llerena Recruited to Illegally Obtain Oxycodone Pills
Llerena then paid his recruits, usually via Zelle, for the oxycodone pills before reselling the pills on the street. Llerena was personally responsible for distributing 3,735 oxycodone pills.
Llerena pled guilty to conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance. A sentencing date has not been set. Llerena faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; United States Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida; Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda Bennett; DEA Special Agent in Charge Miles Aley, Miami Field Division; and FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles made the announcement.
HHS-OIG, DEA, and FBI investigated the case.
Trial Attorney Angela Benoit of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Jacqueline DerOvanesian for the Southern District of Florida are prosecuting the case.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Florida Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Opioid Distribution Conspiracy

Today, Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) and a bipartisan group of 73 members called on the House Appropriations Committee to provide an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental appropriations for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) for Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27). 
 
In the letter, led by New Hampshire Congressman Chris Pappas, the members wrote, “As the war with Iran remains unresolved, energy prices are expected to keep rising, with heating oil up 60% since February. LIHEAP’s $4 billion in funding for the last fiscal year would fall significantly short in meeting the needs of American families this fiscal year.”
 
“LIHEAP is a critical lifeline for low- and moderate-income individuals, but even if your household qualifies, LIHEAP does not provide guaranteed security. Five out of six families who qualify for LIHEAP receive no financial assistance due to the program’s woefully underfunded status. When adjusting for inflation, LIHEAP funding is lower now than it was in 1981 when the program was first created. If LIHEAP was funded at the same level as it was 45 years ago, the program would have received nearly $7 billion in FY27,” they continued.
 
“Emergency LIHEAP assistance is urgently needed as winter weather approaches and colder temperatures have already begun. Families should not have to choose between staying warm and purchasing other essential items like food, medication, or rent. Congress must act and not leave families in the cold,” they concluded. 
 
LIHEAP helps low-income individuals and families pay for heating and cooling and mitigates the impacts of rising energy costs and extreme weather events. Across the nation, LIHEAP helps nearly 6 million households afford their energy bills,including more than 45,000 households in Maine, but Secretary Kennedy’s decision last year to fire all LIHEAP staff last year and President Trump’s repeated demand to cut all funding for the program has put this assistance at risk. In response, Pingree and 89 of her Congressional colleagues in called for the protection of LIHEAP and the rehiring of all HHS staff who manage the LIHEAP program that were fired in April 2025. 
 
Last week, Pingree and a group of 24 Members of Congress representing Northeastern states pressed the Department of Energy (DOE) to take immediate action to address the rapidly rising cost of heating oil, which has surged around 60 percent since the start of President Trump’s war in Iran.
 
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed crude oil from $72 to over $100 a barrel, causing a massive increase in heating oil costs in the United States. American families that rely on heating oil are projected to pay about $600 more to keep their homes warm this winter than last year. In Maine, which uses more residential heating oil per capita than any other U.S. state, the statewide average price of heating oil recently hit a record $6.02 a gallon—marking an 80% increase over last year.
 
Pingree is a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee and has long fought to protect and fully fund LIHEAP. 
 
 
###
title: Pingree Joins Bipartisan Call to Increase Home Heating Assistance Funding

Justice Department Sues State of California over Voter List
Note: view complaint here.
The Justice Department, working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), today filed a complaint against the State of California over its voter list after determining that more than 20,000 people who are likely aliens are registered to vote in California. Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot. It is unlawful for aliens to vote in federal elections.
“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation’s representative system of government. The Department of Justice will continue working to uncover cases of voter fraud, hold fraudsters accountable, and restore trust in American elections.”
“It is unlawful for noncitizens to vote in federal elections,” said Secretary Markwayne Mullin of DHS. “The Department of Homeland Security and our federal partners reviewed publicly available California voter-registration files and compared relevant records with federal immigration data to identify alien registrants. This preliminary analysis has identified a significant number of individuals in California who are likely noncitizens and appear to be registered to vote; the analysis and review remain ongoing. This is completely unacceptable — as even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen and undermines our elections. DHS is committed to identifying unlawful voting, protecting the integrity of federal elections, and ensuring that only eligible American citizens elect America’s leaders.”
“The law is clear, aliens in the United States cannot vote in federal elections,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “What our complaint alleges is that California is facilitating unlawful voting by knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. This needs to stop.”
“California election officials were given an opportunity to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls and to sequester ballots returned from suspected ineligible voters. They refused,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “We are taking California to federal court to demand that the votes of American citizens not be diluted by noncitizens.”
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), in coordination with federal partners, analyzed publicly available voter-registration records to identify potential indicators that aliens may have registered to vote, cast ballots, or received election-related mail. The Department of Justice has filed a complaint against the State of California alleging that these individuals, who are likely noncitizens, registered to vote and/or voted in a federal election. HSI and its federal partners used multiple data-enrichment and verification methods to assess whether the individuals identified were likely aliens.
title: Justice Department Sues State of California over Voter List

text:
Read my Op-Ed in The Portland Press Herald
Between the mountains of snow, the waves of bitter cold and the occasional Nor’easter, we Mainers are no strangers to harsh winters.
This winter could be one of the hardest in recent memory. And not because of the weather. The statewide average price of heating oil just hit a record $6.02 a gallon. As of Sept. 28, it was still averaging $5.96 — up nearly 79% from the same week last year. At today’s price, a 250-gallon fill-up costs about $1,490 — an expense many Maine families will face more than once this winter.
Meanwhile, gas prices are hovering around $4.40 per gallon as of Sept. 25, according to Maine Public.
As if all this wasn’t awful enough, the number of Mainers receiving assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has fallen by 13% — 13,000 people in all, including 7,000 children. Another 31,000 Mainers are projected to lose MaineCare coverage over the next year.
Add it all up and this winter is going to put an enormous strain on Maine families — especially those who can least afford it.
This looming crisis is the result of choices President Trump and congressional Republicans made. Choices they continue to defend.
Let’s back up to July 4, 2025, when the president signed his hallmark legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, into law.
The “Big Ugly Bill” is a more accurate name. It slashed Medicaid by $1.2 trillion and SNAP by $211 billion over the next decade, all while handing hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks to the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations.
Far from offsetting those devastating cuts, the Big Ugly Bill’s ludicrous tax breaks are projected to increase federal deficits by $4.6 trillion, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also handed $175 billion to the Department of Homeland Security, helping turbocharge the Trump administration’s cruel immigration enforcement agenda and bringing chaos and violence to communities across the country. That includes Maine, where an ICE agent shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13.
The young father was not the target of ICE’s operation that morning. He had no criminal history, and we don’t have body camera footage of the shooting. His family has still not been contacted by the federal government and is still waiting for a full accounting of what happened. 
This bill will go down as one of the most irresponsible, destructive, and costly pieces of legislation in American history. Not just in terms of its fiscal recklessness, but its human toll as well: nearly 13 million fewer people enrolled in Medicaid by 2034 and roughly 2.4 million fewer people receiving SNAP in an average month, according to CBO estimates. Its consequences will reach every community in America, in shuttered rural hospitals, overwhelmed food banks and increased costs for state and local governments.
The Big Ugly Bill alone would have been devastating enough for Maine. Then Trump’s reckless, unauthorized war of choice in Iran has kicked every one of these crises into overdrive. In the nearly eight months since the war began — a conflict Trump insisted wouldn’t last more than a few weeks — the global economy has been thrown into turmoil.
The on-again, off-again closure of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping chokepoints, has sent energy prices skyrocketing — and disrupted the flow of goods around the world. When the world’s energy supply gets squeezed, everyone pays more. In a state like Maine, where a colder-than-average winter can mean the difference between keeping the heat on and putting on extra layers just to stay warm, the potential consequences are catastrophic.
None of this had to happen. These crises have been created or made worse by Trump’s policies — and by congressional Republicans’ refusal to push back on the president and stand up for their constituents.
And now, with Americans staring down record energy costs, Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early for a seven-week campaign recess. Rather than staying to work on the many challenges facing our nation, Republicans tucked tail and left.
Republicans could’ve chosen to help you. They chose to help the already-rich get even richer — and to give an army of masked, heavily armed and utterly unaccountable ICE agents virtually unlimited resources to terrorize our communities.
My Democratic colleagues and I have been fighting them every step of the way. We’ve voted against these devastating cuts. We’ve introduced legislation to protect healthcare and food assistance. We’ve demanded accountability for an administration that continues to put its deeply unpopular agenda ahead of the people it’s supposed to serve.
And we are demanding action on the heating crisis: end the war in Iran, protect the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, reverse changes to the Home Owner Managing Energy Savings Rebates and High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate programs and reinstate the energy efficiency tax credits Republicans eliminated. Speaker Johnson should call the House back to Washington so Congress can get to work.
We will keep fighting — at every turn, and for as long as it takes. Because Mainers deserve better. They deserve a government that makes their lives more affordable — not one that cuts their healthcare and food assistance, sends energy prices through the roof and hands massive tax breaks to the people who need them least.
Mainers have survived plenty of hard winters. But the hardships coming this winter are the result of decisions made by Republicans in Washington, who would rather leave town than fix the problems they created.
title: Op-Ed: Mainers are in for a harsh winter— thanks to Republicans

text:
Norcross, local officials break ground on long-awaited third lane for Atlantic City Expressway
GLOUCESTER TOWNSHIP – Congressman Donald Norcross (NJ-01) yesterday joined local and state officials to break ground on the construction of a third lane for the Atlantic City Expressway (ACE) in Gloucester and Camden counties. Upon completion, it will be the culmination of a broader highway widening project that began in 2008.
“Safer roads and less waiting in traffic are goals everyone can get behind, regardless of their political stripes,” Norcross said. “The Atlantic City Expressway is one of the most heavily used roads for residents and visitors of South Jersey alike. I’ve suffered through its congestion my whole life, and have been advocating for its widening since my days in the state legislature. I’m extremely excited to see this long-needed improvement project finally break ground.”
The Atlantic City Expressway runs between Washington Township and Atlantic City, connecting the Philadelphia metro area with the Southern Jersey Shore. Despite serving as the primary roadway for an average of 45,000 daily residents and visitors alike, the highway suffers the second lowest “level of service” grade possible from the New Jersey Department of Transportation and sees a significant number of crashes annually – particularly around the Route 42 interchange.
To relieve congestion and make the ACE safer, the state constructed a third lane in the section closest to Atlantic City between 2008 and 2014. Planning for the northern section to be widened began in 2022, and is expected to be completed in three phases between 2029 and 2031 at the cost of roughly $400 million.
Benefits of the new lane will include fewer accidents due to the freer flow of traffic, reduced air and noise pollution, and faster travel times across the region.
Norcross’ advocacy for road safety dates back to his service in the state legislature. In addition to his longstanding calls for the northern portion of the ACE to be widened, in 2011, he introduced legislation that would raise fines on drivers who created unsafe traffic patterns by failing to return to the right lane of the highway after passing another driver. Norcross’ bill was signed into law in 2013.
title: Norcross, local officials break ground on long-awaited third lane for Atlantic City Expressway

text:
Rep. Torres Announces Power To The Players Act, Legislation to Ensure Gamers Own Their Games
Today, Rep. Ritchie Torres (NY-15) announced he will introduce the Power To The Players Act, legislation that would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations protecting consumers’ ability to own and play the video games they purchase.
Over the past few years, video game companies have moved toward digital-only games and consoles, removing the option to buy or use physical games. These digital games are often sold as revocable licenses rather than owned outright, leaving players dependent on the company’s continued support. NBA 2K25 is a clear example. The game, which retailed for $69.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the All-Star Edition, will be delisted from digital storefronts on October 30 and will have its online servers shut down on December 31, only two years after its initial release. No consumer should have a game they paid for pulled out from under them on a company’s arbitrary timeline.
“When you pay for a game, you should own it,” said Rep. Torres. “Consumers must have the right to own, the right to play, and the right to transfer the games they buy. A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale. Families in the Bronx and across the country save up to buy these games, and they deserve better than a license that can vanish at any time. The Power To The Players Act ensures consumers own what they buy and can keep playing long after a company moves on.”
Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it. Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down.
The legislation aims to close the gap between buying a game and owning it. By preserving consumers’ ability to own and resell their games, the bill would ensure that players can keep playing the games they paid for with friends and family for years to come.
title: Rep. Torres Announces Power To The Players Act, Legislation to Ensure Gamers Own Their Games

EPA completes cleanup of former hospital site in Colorado
EPA addressed asbestos-containing material and demolition debris in Walsenburg
DENVER – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced the completion of a response action in Walsenburg, Colorado, to clean up and properly dispose of asbestos-containing material (ACM) and fire-damaged debris from a former hospital site and abandoned residence. The cleanup removed 1,520 cubic yards of ACM and contaminated debris, reducing the risk of asbestos fibers being released into the environment and helping prepare the site for future redevelopment.
“Cleaning up contaminated properties is essential to protecting human health and the environment, and it plays a critical role in community revitalization," said EPA Regional Administrator Cyrus Western. "By removing asbestos and debris from this site, EPA is reducing risks today and helping create a safer, stronger future for Walsenburg."
Following an October 2023 fire at the former hospital, Huerfano County Economic Development used an EPA Brownfields assessment grant to complete environmental site assessments. In July 2026, at the request of Huerfano County and Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE), EPA initiated an emergency response removal at the former Lamme Hospital site.
"Huerfano County is grateful to the US EPA for their assistance cleaning up the old Lamme Hospital,” said Huerfano County Board Chair Karl Sporleder. “This effort has removed hazardous materials from the property and marks an important step toward transforming this corner into a safer, more vibrant space for the community and downtown businesses.”
EPA mobilized to the site on September 17, and the response was completed on October 10. During the response EPA conducted particulate and asbestos air monitoring to ensure asbestos fibers did not migrate off site and ACM debris was transported for disposal to a permitted landfill in Pueblo.
By removing ACM and contaminated debris from the site, the cleanup reduced the potential for asbestos fibers to become airborne and protected the community from the health risks associated with asbestos exposure.
EPA and CDPHE remain available to respond to questions and will coordinate with Huerfano County if needed. For more information, please visit EPA's Old Hospital Asbestos webpage.
Learn more about EPA’s emergency response program.
title: EPA completes cleanup of former hospital site in Colorado
